text: You've already learned penetration testing methodology elsewhere in this path: a defined scope, written authorization, rules of engagement, and a formal report. AI red-teaming is that exact same discipline, applied to an AI system. It is not a developer idly trying to get a chatbot to say something embarrassing — it's a planned, authorized exercise against a specific, in-scope system, with defined objectives and a written report at the end.

A real engagement works through a test plan built from the risk categories this course has already covered, now exercised against the live system. Can prompt injection override the system's own instructions? Can the engagement extract system prompts, out-of-scope retrieved documents, or fragments of memorized training data? Can crafted input push the model into producing content its own policy should block? And if the system can call tools or take actions, can an attacker get it to take one outside its intended authority?

What makes this testing rather than attacking is the paperwork around it. Rules of engagement name the exact system and environment in scope, carry written authorization from whoever owns the risk, run inside a time-boxed window, and define test categories before any testing starts. Every prompt and every response gets logged as evidence — the same evidentiary discipline a penetration test report depends on.

None of this is invented. MITRE ATLAS catalogs real adversary tactics and techniques against machine learning systems, mirroring MITRE ATT&CK. NIST's Generative AI Profile names red-teaming explicitly as a method under the framework's Measure function. Microsoft's AI Red Team publishes its own methodology, and open-source tooling like PyRIT automates large batches of adversarial test prompts. The engagement itself follows the familiar pentest lifecycle: scope and authorize, design test cases from those frameworks, execute and log, report findings tied to evidence, then retest to confirm the fix actually holds.

That's the whole picture: red-teaming as a formal, repeatable assessment, not improvisation. Next, you'll build the threat model that tells a red team exactly what to prioritize for a given system — its data sensitivity, its autonomy, and its trust boundary.
